newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary sets up Jewish survivors' foundation.
newsitem.headline: Hungary sets up Jewish survivors' foundation.

text.p: Hungary's Jewish community, overcoming years of delay, inaugurated a public foundation on Tuesday to aid the country's estimated 20,000 to 40,000 Holocaust survivors.

"This is a historic moment," Gusztav Zoltai, managing director of the Confederation of Jewish Communities in Hungary (MAZSIHISZ), said at a ceremony held in a meeting hall in the Jewish community's office building in Budapest.
"After 50 years we can win the very little pieces of our claims," Zoltai said. "But it is a good example for other European countries."
Zoltai spoke at the first meeting of the Hungarian Jewish Heritage Foundation, which was established by an act of Parliament and approved by the government earlier this month.

After years of often bitter debate between the government and the Jewish community, and within the Jewish community itself, the government agreed to establish the foundation and to give it four billion forints ($24 million) of compensation coupons, plus some other property.

Jewish community leaders say that the financial bequest should be sufficient to provide elderly Holocaust survivors, most of whom are now in their 70s or 80s, with supplemental pensions of about 5,000 forints ($30) a month.
"It's actually a very big amount because it's about 1.2 billion forints ($6.8 million) a year," one community official said earlier.

But one big unknown is how many survivors of the Nazi Holocaust are still alive in Hungary, which at the outbreak of World War Two had the second largest Jewish community in central Europe, after Poland.
"It could be 20,000 or possibly 40,000," Zoltai said. "In two or three months we will know."
"It is unfortunate that this has taken so long because every year 600 to 800 die and they are all Holocaust survivors," he added.

Jewish officials said the 21-member public foundation is the first of its kind in central Europe to deal with the issue of providing compensation for Jewish property confiscated under both the fascist and communist eras.
It will also have the role of promoting Jewish culture, education and religion in Hungary, whose 80,000 to 100,000 Jews now constitute the biggest Jewish community in the region.
